The Judgment of the Court was delivered by

Krishnan Ramasamy, J.:— The suit have been filed by the plaintiffs for the relief of permanent injunction and such other reliefs more fully described in the prayer portion of this judgment.

2. The first plaintiff originally started trading under the name and style of Abishek Enterprises. The first plaintiff was engaged in the business of manufacturing and marketing spices and condiments under the trademark AACHI. The mark was first adopted in the year 1995. The trading style of the first plaintiff was subsequently changed to Naveen Enterprises which was a partnership firm of the first plaintiff along with his mother in law Mrs. Rani Pandian. This partnership was dissolved on 31.03.2007 as evidenced by Ex. P4. Subsequently, AACHI Spices and Foods was formed. The first plaintiff trading as AACHI Spices and Foods was registered under the CST on 28.12.2006 and 03.01.2007 respectively Ex. P6. Both Abhishek Enterprises and Naveen Products assigned the trademark AACHI used by them in favour of the first plaintiff as evidenced by Exs. P3 & P4. With the growth of the organization Nazareth Foods Pvt. Ltd., was incorporated to undertake the manufacturing activities. One of the marks used by the plaintiffs for Kulambu Chilly Powder since 10.05.2002 was applied on 01.11.2004, after the mark acquired distinctiveness. The registration was granted in favour of the first plaintiff and the first plaintiff is the registered proprietor of the trademark AACHI as depicted in Ex. P16 and as registered under Ex. P17.

3. The second plaintiff was incorporated to both market and manufacture the AACHI products of the first plaintiff. The incorporation certificate of the second plaintiff is Ex. P2. The second plaintiff is the licensee of the first plaintiff. Exs. P9 and P14 are the licenses granted by the first plaintiff in favour of the second plaintiff. The certificate of commercial tax of the second plaintiff is Ex. P8. Aachi Masala Foods Pvt. Ltd., also assigned the Trademark AACHI in favour of the first plaintiff in Ex. P7.

4. Aachi Spices and Foods Private Limited was incorporated under Ex. P11. Aachi Spices and Foods Private Limited also uses the trademark AACHI in the course of trade under license from the first plaintiff Ex. P13.

5. The plaintiffs have been manufacturing and marketing spices and other food products since 1995 for the past 25 years under the trademark AACHI. The plaintiffs are manufacturing spices and condiments in 433 packaging as seen in Ex. P10. The turnover of the plaintiffs in the year 2006 was about Rs. 230 crores. The plaintiffs have advertised the trademark AACHI as seen in Ex. P15. The mark AACHI acquired tremendous reputation and goodwill and the trade and public associate the trademark AACHI only with the plaintiffs. In fact, the mark AACHI has been registered in several countries around the world as seen in Ex. P18.

6. While so, the plaintiffs came to know of the use of the trademark Jaya Rani Masala with respect to Kulambu Chilly Powder in July 2013. The plaintiffs came forward with the above suit in September 2013. On 04.11.2013, exparte order of [Page 48] interim injunction was granted in favour of the plaintiffs. The order of interim injunction is still in force.

7. After the admission of the suit, the suit summons was served on the sole defendant on 14.11.2013. In spite of the service of the suit summons, the defendant failed to appear before this Court. Therefore, the sole defendant was set ex-parte… vide order dated 10.07.2019 and the suit was directed to be placed before the learned Additional Master for recording ex-parte evidence. Before the learned Additional Master, on behalf of the plaintiff one Mr. B. Gnanasambandain, was examined as P.W. 1 and Exs. P1 to P19 were marked.

9. Heard the learned counsel for the plaintiffs and also gone through the averments in the plaint and the proof affidavit and also perused the Ex. P. 1 to P. 19.

10. On perusal of Ex. P18, this Court is of the view that the trademark ‘Aachi’ of the plaintiffs is a registered trademark. plaintiffs' registration in Class 30 is vide Trademark No. 1318495 and the Legal Use Certificate [Trademark Registration Certificate] for this has been marked as Ex. P17. Further, the plaintiffs also filed their photo copy of the name board and the same is marked as Ex. P. 16 and the defendant's photo copy of the name board as Ex. P. 19. The trademark adopted by the defendant is both visually, phonetically and deceptively similar to that of the plaintiffs. On perusal of Exs. P16 and P19, it is seen that the defendant is not only copying the trademark of the plaintiffs ‘Aachi’ but also copying the colour scheme and get up. Therefore, this Court found that the defendant's copying the plaintiffs trademark ‘Aachi’ will amount to infringement of the trademark, as stated in Section 29 of the Trademarks Act. Accordingly, the plaintiffs proved the claim. Therefore, the plaintiffs are entitled to the decree as prayed for.

11. Learned counsel for plaintiffs requests this Commercial Division to consider imposing compensatory costs/exemplary costs on defendant in the light of conduct of the defendant which has been referred to supra. Learned counsel also pointed out that the defendant has compelled plaintiffs to carry this matter for a substantial [Page 50] time in this Court, expending money, energy and effort. Reference to Section 35-A The Civil Procedure Code, 1908 (‘C.P.C.’ for brevity) as amended by The Commercial Courts Act, 2015 (‘said Act’ for brevity) was also made. Section 35-A provides for compensatory costs in respect of false or vexatious defences. In the instant case, defendant pursuing the trademark registration applications on the teeth of opposition, but evading conventional modes of service, compelling substituted service and not appearing before this Court even after service being effected through substituted service, in the considered view of this Commercial Division will qualify as a vexatious defence (within the meaning of Section 35-A of amended CPC as amended by said Act) as it is a vexatious manner of defending a suit. Be that as it may, in the light of the trajectory and in the light of the defendant's approach to this suit, this Commercial Division is convinced that it is appropriate to impose compensatory costs of Rs. 50,000 (Rupees Fifty Thousand only) on the defendant. Plaintiffs will obviously be entitled to costs as the plaintiff has incurred substantial expenditure in carrying this suit to its logical end.

12. Suit is decreed with costs and compensatory costs as set out supra.
